title: Attention kernel optimization profiling: FlashAttention vs paged attention vs fused ops — bottleneck analysis
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures the results and running notes from a set of microbenchmarks and end-to-end traces designed to identify bottlenecks in our attention kernels. We compared FlashAttention implementations, our paged-attention prototype, and fused-ops (self-attn + projection fusion) variants across A100-80GB and H100 instances. The goal: give clear recommendations for which kernel variants to enable by default for low-latency serving and where to apply runtime routing/heuristics in the serving stack.

Background / Motivation:
- Attention is the dominant compute pattern for autoregressive and encoder-decoder workloads. Small inefficiencies multiply at serving scale.
- Recent kernel innovations (FlashAttention v1/v2, paged attention for long contexts, and fused ops that reduce memory traffic) promise big throughput/latency wins but have nuanced tradeoffs across seq-len, batch-size, and GPU micro-architecture.
- We need SLO-safe defaults for hosted and dedicated deployments and rules for automatic fallbacks (e.g., fall back to standard xformers when batch/seq combos degrade).

Testbed and methodology:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (PCIe) and NVIDIA H100 SXM (80GB) nodes used. Drivers/CUDA: 535.x on H100, 520.x on A100.
- Models: 7B dense transformer (GPT-like) and a 13B variant for higher memory pressure tests. Models converted with the same tokenizer and random weights (we care about perf, not accuracy).
- Kernels evaluated: FlashAttention v1, FlashAttention v2 (where fused GEMM+softmax paths exist), paged-attention (our internal staged-KV caching + paged memory access), fused-ops (self-attn + out-proj fused CUDA kernels), and baseline xformers/cuda-native aten attention.
- Measurements: 1) per-token tail latency p50/p90/p99, 2) tokens/sec throughput for steady-state streaming with continuous generation, 3) GPU metrics via nsight-cu (SM utilization, achieved occupancy, L2 BW utilization, DRAM throughput), 4) CUDA kernel time breakdown from nvprof/nvtx ranges.
- Workloads: short context (seq=64), medium (seq=512), long (seq=2048). Batch sizes {1,4,8,16} depending on seq len and GPU memory. Each experiment run 10 warmup iterations + 100 measured iterations.

Key findings (high level):
1) FlashAttention v2 consistently reduces per-token latency for short-to-medium sequences (seq<=512). p99 improved ~20-45% vs baseline for batch=1 on H100, slightly less on A100.
2) For long sequences (seq>=1024), paged-attention reduces peak memory usage and allows larger batch sizes but introduces extra bookkeeping overhead that increases per-token latency for small batch sizes — tradeoff beneficial when memory-bound and batch>1.
3) Fused-ops provide notable wall-time improvements (10-25%) when projection and attention kernels can be coalesced, primarily by reducing global memory traffic and kernel-launch overhead; gains are higher on H100 due to better tensor-core fusion support.
4) Memory bandwidth and L2 utilization are primary bottlenecks for medium/long sequences; SM utilization is often suboptimal (<55%) when using paged attention due to serialization in page management code paths.
5) End-to-end serving latency sometimes dominated by non-kernel overheads (encoder/decoder reshapes, KV cache copy costs, CUDA stream synchronization) — kernel wins are necessary but not sufficient.

Representative numbers (H100, 7B, batch=1):
- seq=64: baseline p50=12.1ms p99=18.8ms; FlashAttn-v2 p50=8.7ms p99=11.4ms (≈40% p99 reduction).
- seq=512: baseline throughput=620 toks/s; FlashAttn-v2 throughput=880 toks/s; fused-ops throughput=980 toks/s.
- seq=2048: baseline OOM at batch=4; paged-attn allows batch=2 with throughput 140 toks/s (steady), FlashAttn (no paging) only batch=1 possible.

Profiling notes / interesting traces:
- nvtx ranges showed that for seq=512 most time spent in two kernels: `attn_softmax` and `kv_gather`. FlashAttention fused the softmax+matmul reducing two kernels into one path — fewer launches and much better memory locality.
- For paged-attention, we observed frequent small memcpy/device-to-device page transfers causing PCIe stalls on A100 tests when memory oversubscription occurred. H100 with NVLink mitigated that effect.
- Kernel timings on H100: fused-ops kernel had longer single-kernel time but overall lower end-to-end due to removal of subsequent projection kernel and reduced synchronization.
- L2 bandwidth: paged-attention increases L2 working set churn; FlashAttention lowers L2 pressure by streaming data within shared memory/tiles.

Bottleneck analysis by dimension:
- Short seq (<=128), batch<=4: compute-bound on tensor cores; FlashAttn-v2 wins due to fused softmax+matmul and lower kernel-launch overhead.
- Medium seq (256–768): mixed compute+bandwidth; fused-ops + FlashAttn recommended; monitor L2 and DRAM BW and limit batch size to prevent paging.
- Long seq (>1024): memory-bound. Paged-attention or KV-paging required; expect higher per-token latency for batch=1. Use paged-attn when memory prevents required batch sizes or when latency SLO allows per-token increase but preserves throughput.

Regression risks / correctness notes:
- FlashAttention v2 implementations must be validated against numerical edge cases (padding masks, causal masking) — we saw small fp16 underflow differences in internal tests. Add unit tests for masked softmax equivalence with fp32 reference for critical paths.
- Paged-attention introduces more complex concurrency patterns: race/lock issues in page eviction observed in early prototype; these were fixed by a per-stream page-lock model but needs more fuzz testing.
- Fused kernels may obscure gradient shapes for training; not relevant for serving but verify that saved kernels don't introduce ABI mismatches with our operator registry.

Operational recommendations (short):
1) Default for hosted low-latency routes (batch<=4, seq<=512): enable FlashAttention v2 + fused-ops. Add auto-flag that disables paged-attn for these routes.
2) For routes with long context needs: enable paged-attention as an opt-in capability; route based on memory pressure heuristic (estimated tokens in-flight + kv-size).
3) Add runtime telemetry and fallback: if p99 increases >20% after switching kernel, auto-fallback to baseline kernel for 5 minutes and trigger alert.
4) Add unit/integration tests for masking and numerics; add a nightly perf job that runs the microbench suite against A100 and H100 images to detect regressions.

Implementation action items / TODOs:
- PR#1423: integrate FlashAttention-v2 build flags into our runtime build (owner: Noah). Blockers: CUDA 535+ integration on CI images.
- SERVERTIME-378: add paged-attention opt-in route config + eviction debug logs (owner: Elena).
- Benchmark harness: capture nvprof/nvtx ranges automatically and upload artifacts for 24-hour retention (owner: Marcus).
- Add telemetry counters: kernel_version, seq_len, batch_size, kernel_time_ms (p50/p90/p99) into console/trace pipeline.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quantization interaction: how do 4-bit quantization kernels affect FlashAttention/fused-ops performance and numerics? Need targeted tests (priority medium).
- Cost model: derive tokens/sec per-$ for each kernel combo on A100 vs H100 to feed optimizer.
- Edge cases for multi-tenant Dedicated: how does sharing GPU across small inference workers (many small batches) change relative benefits? Do we need a different default?

Appendix: commands and snippet used for profiling (run from perf VM)
- Microbench binary (simple): 
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python perf/bench_attention.py --model 7b --seq 512 --batch 1 --kernel flashattn_v2 --iters 110 --warmup 10 --nvtx

- nvprof capture: 
  nv-nsight-cu-cli --export-profile profile.gz --target-processes all --section 'Launch' python perf/bench_attention.py --...

- Example nvtx slice summary (trimmed):
  [nvtx] attn_forward (kernel): 6.7ms
  [nvtx] kv_gather (kernel): 2.1ms
  [nvtx] out_proj (kernel): 1.8ms

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is a working summary; numbers are from lab runs, not production workloads. Expect variation across clouds and driver versions. Please review the suggested operational heuristics and sign off on PR#1423 to proceed with staged rollout on a small fleet (canaries) before global enable.
